title: How do you handle concurrency conflicts in EF Core?
description: RowVersion tokens, DbUpdateConcurrencyException handling, and optimistic vs pessimistic locking.

data.text: **Question:** How do you handle concurrency conflicts in EF Core?

EF Core uses **optimistic concurrency** by default: it never locks rows for you. You mark a property as a **concurrency token** — typically a SQL Server `rowversion` column via `IsRowVersion()` — and EF adds `WHERE Id = @id AND RowVersion = @original` to every UPDATE/DELETE. If zero rows are affected, someone else changed the record first: EF throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`, and you resolve it (reload, merge, or tell the user). Pessimistic locking (held locks) exists at the database level but is not EF's model.

**Setting it up:**
- Fluent API: `entity.Property(o => o.RowVersion).IsRowVersion();` (SQL Server auto-generates `rowversion`)
- Any property can be a token: `IsConcurrencyToken()` — e.g. a `UpdatedAt` timestamp or a `Counter` you expect to change only by your write
- Client-side original values come from the snapshot EF took when the entity was loaded — another reason load-modify-save wants a tracked entity

**What happens on conflict:**
- UPDATE/DELETE matches nothing → `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`
- `exception.Entries` gives you the entities involved; each entry holds **current** (your) and **original** (database) values
- Resolution strategies:
  - **Reload & inform:** `entry.GetDatabaseValuesAsync()` — compare, show the other user's version, let them re-apply
  - **Last-write-wins:** set `entry.OriginalValues` to current and retry — acceptable for coarse fields, dangerous for money/inventory
  - **Field-level merge:** reapply only your changed fields onto fresh database values
  - **Custom:** record an audit entry of both versions

**Optimistic vs pessimistic:**
- Optimistic: no locks, high read throughput, conflicts are rare and handled in code — the default for web apps
- Pessimistic (`SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK)` / `sp_getapplock` / `pg_advisory_lock`): needed when conflicts are frequent or the operation can't be retried (seat reservation, counter increments, non-idempotent external calls)
- For simple increments, a single set-based statement (`UPDATE ... SET Qty = Qty - 1`) sidesteps read-modify-write entirely

data.title: RowVersion token and conflict resolution

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing EF does **not** lock — and what optimistic concurrency means in practice
- Hands-on familiarity with IsRowVersion and DbUpdateConcurrencyException
- Conscious conflict-resolution choices (reload/merge vs last-write-wins), not swallowed exceptions
- When to drop to pessimistic/set-based approaches instead

items: Catching DbUpdateConcurrencyException and just retrying blindly — the same conflict returns, and blind retries hide data loss
Attaching a modified entity with stale original values (Update on a detached POCO) — the WHERE clause uses wrong originals
Using last-write-wins on inventory, prices, or balances
Thinking optimistic concurrency prevents deadlocks — it doesn't; it converts lost updates into exceptions
Marking every property as a concurrency token — conflicts on fields nobody contends for
Forgetting deletes: DELETE carries the token too and can throw the same exception
How would you implement a seat reservation where double-booking is unacceptable?
What concurrency strategy would you use across two services writing to the same table?
Is a timestamp column as good as rowversion? What are the pitfalls?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: EF is optimistic by default: the token rides in the UPDATE/DELETE WHERE clause
IsRowVersion() on SQL Server; IsConcurrencyToken() for app-managed tokens
DbUpdateConcurrencyException → reload, merge, or last-write-wins — by choice
Use pessimistic or set-based writes when conflicts are frequent or non-retryable
data.takeaway: Concurrency conflicts are a design decision: detect them with a token, then resolve them deliberately — never by swallowing the exception.
